1	# AGENTS.md - Bot Instructions
2	
3	## Project Structure
4	
5	This project uses **two separate jj-git repos**:
6	
7	1. **App repo** (`/` — project root): the project's generated
8	   artifact — code, prose, image, song, whatever it produces.
9	2. **Bot session repo** (`/.claude/`): Contains Claude Code session data.
10	
11	Both repos are managed with `jj` (Jujutsu), which coexists with git.
12	
13	**Committing vs pushing.** Default to `vc-x1 push` — it commits and
14	publishes both repos together, each carrying one `ochid:` pointing at
15	the other (see [Cycle Protocol](#cycle-protocol) and
16	[ochid trailers](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). Use a bare
17	`jj commit` (see [jj Basics](#jj-basics)) only when:
18	
19	- the change will never be published — no `ochid:`;
20	- the commit will be squashed away before its series is pushed
21	  (loop-and-squash) — no `ochid:`; it disappears in the squash;
22	- the commit will be pushed later as a non-top commit — `jj commit`
23	  and add its `ochid:` now, because `vc-x1 push` stamps only the
24	  topmost commit it pushes, never the ancestors.
25	
26	**What "commit" and "push" mean.** In an instruction, "commit",
27	"push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push` — land *and*
28	publish — unless stated otherwise. A bare `jj commit` is asked for
29	by name: "local commit", "save locally", "just `jj commit`" (the
30	cases above). So the spoken default is publish; the local-only
31	save is the named exception. The approval around a push —
32	interactive by default, waived only by an explicit scoped
33	delegation — is the cycle protocol's
34	[Pushing policy](notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy).
35	
36	## Repo Paths (relative from project root)
37	
38	- App repo: `.` (project root)
39	- Bot session repo: `.claude`
40	  (symlink from `~/.claude/projects/<path-to-project-root>/.claude`)
41	
42	## Working Directory
43	
44	Prefer staying in the project root. Use `-R` flags or absolute paths
45	to target other directories rather than `cd`. If `cd` seems necessary,
46	discuss with the user first — losing track of cwd causes subtle
47	command failures downstream.
48	
49	When invoking shell commands, prefer the shortest unambiguous path —
50	usually relative to cwd (`ls notes/`, not
51	`ls /home/wink/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1/notes/`). Long absolute paths
52	clutter the transcript without adding information. Out-of-workspace
53	paths (`/tmp/...`, `~/.config/...`) stay absolute. Read/Edit/Write
54	tool args also stay absolute — that's a tool-boundary constraint,
55	not a stylistic choice.
56	
57	Run **one command per shell invocation** — don't bundle several
58	steps into a single compound script (`a && b; c`). Bundling hides
59	which step produced which output and makes a failure ambiguous;
60	executing one at a time keeps the details visible and reviewable.
61	Exceptions are a genuine pipeline (`grep | sort`) or a tight,
62	inseparable pair where the join is the point.
63	
64	## File reads — read the slice you need
65	
66	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the
67	slice your task needs; grep or read further on demand.
68	
69	- **`notes/todo.md`** (the routine acquaint read) — first
70	  ~60 lines covers intro + `## In Progress` + the top of the
71	  ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
72	  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`; read
73	  further only when chasing a lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a
74	  `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
75	- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`** — the long-tail backlog
76	  (lower-priority entries below the ranked `## Todo`). Read
77	  only when picking up a backlog item; grep to locate it
78	  first.
79	- **`notes/bugs.md`** — the bug list. Small; read whole
80	  when triaging a bug or chasing the `## Bugs` pointer in
81	  todo.md.
82	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`** —
83	  historical / append-mostly. Scan headings first
84	  (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only
85	  the section you need.
86	
87	**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `notes/todo.md`
88	grows every cycle, so the backlog and bugs live in sibling
89	files rather than inline; the same "slice you need" rule
90	applies to historical files.
91	
92	## Memory
93	
94	Do not use the bot's per-project memory directory
95	(`~/.claude/projects/<path>/memory/`). In a dual-repo setup with
96	AGENTS.md it provides no capability AGENTS.md doesn't already cover,
97	and it loses on discoverability:
98	
99	- **AGENTS.md** — at the repo root, a well-known location for bot
100	  instructions, committed, reviewable, visible to every collaborator
101	  (human or bot).
102	- **Memory directory** — hidden under the user's home, tied to one
103	  machine, invisible to anyone but the bot, never diffed or reviewed.
104	
105	Easy for everyone to find beats convenient for the bot alone. Put
106	durable context in AGENTS.md (or committed `notes/`) instead.
107	
108	## Plain synopsis after technical explanations
109	
110	When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation
111	(measurement theory, statistics, hardware behavior), end it
112	with a short plain-language synopsis — no jargon, no symbols —
113	so the reader can check their understanding against the
114	technical version.
115	
116	**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread;
117	the plain form catches misunderstandings early, when they are
118	cheap.
119	
120	**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (notes
121	link to design.md, which should already lead with the why).
122	Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is
123	already plain needs no synopsis.
124	
125	## Speculation marker
126	
127	Durable text the bot writes — AGENTS.md, `notes/`, commit bodies,
128	chores sections — should stick to observations and direct descriptions
129	of the code or data. If a mechanism, hypothesis, or causal claim
130	enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
131	reader can tell the measured from the inferred.
132	
133	**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader
134	(or the bot on a later session) can pick it up as a known fact when
135	it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction worth keeping visible
136	in the written record.
137	
138	**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no
139	marker. Prefix with "We think ..." (or a close variant like
140	"Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism ("X wins
141	because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal
142	state"), a prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any
143	reasoning not directly supported by the data on hand.
144	
145	## jj Basics
146	
147	**Use jj, not git, for version-control operations** (status, log,
148	diff, commit, push, history rewrite). jj coexists with the git
149	backend, so the repo *can* be driven with raw `git`, but this
150	project's workflow — bookmarks, the working-copy `@` model, ochid
151	trailers — is expressed in jj terms; reaching for `git` invites
152	state that doesn't match the jj documentation here. There is no
153	`jj mv`: to move/rename a tracked file, just `mv` it on disk and
154	jj detects the rename by content.
155	
156	- `jj st -R .` / `jj st -R .claude` — show working copy status
157	- `jj log -R .` / `jj log -R .claude` — show commit log
158	- `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>` — finalize working copy into a commit
159	- `jj describe -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>` — set description without committing
160	- `jj git push --bookmark <name> -R <repo>` — push a bookmark (no
161	  `--allow-new` flag; jj pushes new bookmarks without special flags)
162	- In jj, the working copy (@) is always a mutable commit being edited.
163	  `jj commit` finalizes it and creates a new empty working copy on top.
164	- The `.claude` repo always has uncommitted changes during an active
165	  session because session data updates continuously.
166	- `jj rebase` uses `--onto`/`-o` to name the destination(s).
167	
168	## Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)
169	
170	The cross-reference between the app repo and the `.claude` bot
171	repo is what makes the dual-repo work: every commit points at its
172	counterpart in the other repo, so the "what" (code) and the
173	"why / how" (session) stay linked across time. That pointer is the
174	**ochid** (Other Change ID) git trailer.
175	
176	A **chid** is jj's change ID — a permanent identifier that
177	survives rebases and `describe`s (unlike the commit ID / git SHA,
178	which changes on rewrite). An **ochid** trailer carries the
179	counterpart commit's chid as a workspace-root-relative path:
180	
181	- Paths start with `/` — the workspace root, i.e. the app repo
182	  (vc-template-x1). `/.claude` is the bot session sub-repo.
183	- `ochid: /<chid>` references a change in the **app repo**.
184	- `ochid: /.claude/<chid>` references a change in the **`.claude`
185	  repo**.
186	
187	Trailers are blank-line-separated `key: value` lines at the end of
188	the commit body, using the chid's **12-character** prefix:
189	
190	```
191	ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqowktp   # points to a .claude repo change
192	ochid: /wtpmottvxqzl           # points to an app repo change
193	```
194	
195	How many, and which direction:
196	
197	- **Code-side commits** each carry one
198	  `ochid: /.claude/<.claude-chid>` — the `.claude` change ID.
199	- **The `.claude` commit** carries one `ochid: /<code-chid>` per
200	  code commit in that push. More than one occurs on a Merge
201	  non-ff close-out (one ochid per Work commit in the cycle).
202	
203	Use `vc-x1 chid -s code,bot -L` to capture the change IDs (first
204	line app, second `.claude`).
205	
206	### Resolvability
207	
208	A change ID travels with its commit: a **pushed** commit resolves
209	to the same chid in every clone — cloning the `.claude` repo gave
210	the published `main` tip the same chid as an existing clone. We
211	think jj carries the change ID in the git commit object, so it
212	survives `jj git clone` / fetch.
213	
214	The local-only case is the **working-copy `@`**: jj mints a fresh
215	random chid for `@` in each clone, so an unpushed `@` is never a
216	stable ochid target. This is why a `.claude` ochid names `@-`
217	(the last committed change), not `@`.
218	
219	### .vc-config.toml
220	
221	Each repo contains a `.vc-config.toml` that identifies its
222	location within the workspace, so tools resolve these paths
223	without repeating the workspace path in every trailer:
224	
225	```toml
226	# In vc-template-x1 (workspace root):
227	[workspace]
228	path = "/"
229	
230	# In .claude (sub-repo):
231	[workspace]
232	path = "/.claude"
233	```
234	
235	## Prose form
236	
237	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro
238	that explains the *why* or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet
239	list for the details. Wrap lines at ≤72 cols (bullet continuations
240	indent two spaces). Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs — they hide the
241	structure that bullets make scannable.
242	
243	Surfaces that use this shape:
244	
245	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files —
246	  see [Doc comments](#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
247	- Commit message bodies (both app-repo and session-repo). The
248	  ≤50-col title is the commit-specific add-on; see
249	  [Per-commit flow](notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
250	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` — see
251	  [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
252	- Todo and Done entries in `notes/todo.md` when an entry needs more
253	  than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are still fine.
254	
255	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
256	
257	- **Commit bodies** — bullets are file-by-file: one bullet per file
258	  changed, file plus a one-line gist (e.g.
259	  `README.md: new Overview intro`). Source of truth for the
260	  mechanical edit list.
261	- **Chores / todo / done** — bullets are conceptual (design points,
262	  structural notes, the "what landed and why" at a notch above
263	  file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list —
264	  see [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
265	- **Doc comments** — bullets are whatever structure fits (fields,
266	  cases, invariants).
267	
268	### Problem + plan shape
269	
270	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores section intros, and `## Todo`
271	entries use a sharper form of the same shape:
272	
273	- **Problem statement** (the why) — one or two sentences;
274	  don't pad with intent, don't restate the plan.
275	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when) — formality differs by
276	  surface:
277	  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per
278	    commit — see
279	    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit)
280	    for the per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
281	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering;
282	    formalized only when the entry is picked up into a
283	    cycle.
284	
285	### Semicolons inside bullets
286	
287	A bullet that joins multiple clauses with semicolons (`A; B; C`)
288	is a list hiding inside running prose — break the clauses into
289	sub-bullets so the structure shows. Semicolons in running prose
290	(intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very
291	short clauses or tight pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when
292	breaking would be more noise than signal.
293	
294	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)
295	
296	A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description
297	share a *title* shape — a
298	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/)
299	title over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail. They differ in the
300	title's prefix / marker (below) and in bullet *content* — commit
301	bodies are file-by-file, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet
302	*content* differs by surface" above). The shared template:
303	
304	```
305	<optional - X.Y.Z[-N]> <title>   # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
306	<optional prose intro>
307	  - <optional item>
308	    <optional prose intro>
309	      - <optional sub-item>
310	      ...
311	```
312	
313	The three surfaces apply it as:
314	
315	- **Ladder step** (`notes/todo.md` `## In Progress`): the title is
316	  prefixed with the version — `X.Y.Z-N <title>` — and
317	  carries a `(current)` / `(done)` marker. The bare three-element
318	  `X.Y.Z` (no `-N`) is the close-out step. Detail is bulleted,
319	  never `;`-joined inline.
320	- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no version
321	  prefix — the `##` header *is* the bare title, with a
322	  `Commits: [[ref]]` line first under it (empty until backfilled —
323	  see [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references)).
324	- **Commit description**: no version prefix — the title is the
325	  ≤50-col first line; the body is the prose (file-by-file for the
326	  app repo, per [Per-commit flow](notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow)).
327	
328	The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a
329	step's ladder entry, its chores `##` header, and its commit title
330	line up verbatim — pick the commit title first and reuse it.
331	
332	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a
333	cycle gets its own distinct descriptive title — never one shared
334	cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
335	section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep
336	a cycle's commits collectable with one `git log --grep`, give the
337	step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).
338	
339	## Notes file conventions
340	
341	Conventions the bot follows when writing notes files
342	(`notes/todo.md`, `notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`,
343	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One source
344	of truth lives here; [`notes/README.md`](notes/README.md)
345	points back.
346	
347	### Notes references
348	
349	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render
350	— `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]` for several (comma-separated, not
351	`[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
352	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)`
353	links stay single-bracketed.
354	
355	### Reference numbering
356	
357	Every note file (`todo.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`,
358	`chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a file-local `# References`
359	section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that
360	file — `[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md`
361	are independent slots that may point at completely different
362	URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.
363	
364	Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only
365	meaningful within its file's `# References`. So a `[N]` *citation*
366	(bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another file's number; to cite a target a sibling
367	file references, pick your own next-local slot and define it
368	(the same target may carry a different number in each file). A
369	`[N]` *inside a code span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different — that's
370	a quoted identifier: literal text naming a ref-key (often from
371	another file's namespace), data, not a citation; it needs no
372	definition here. To point at a section of another file from
373	prose, use an inline link with an anchor —
374	`[that section](../chores-07.md#…)` — not a bare number.
375	
376	A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a
377	`/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or `/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may
378	also be a **commit reference** —
379	`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by
380	a section's `Commits:` line. See
381	[Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the
382	why and the exact shape.
383	
384	A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous
385	`[1]..[N]` in first-citation-appearance order — walk the file's
386	prose in document order (`todo.md`: `## Todo` then `## Done`;
387	`chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first
388	`[[N]]` citation appears. This is a file-local rewrite — only
389	that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:` definitions move; every
390	target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` ``
391	code span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone.
392	Do it opportunistically (when the namespace has drifted enough to
393	annoy), not on a schedule: `todo.md` fragments fastest (entries
394	land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate;
395	`chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are append-mostly and only need it
396	after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated slots
397	out of document order).
398	
399	### Markdown anchor links
400	
401	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric
402	characters in place, map remaining spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do
403	**not** collapse adjacent whitespace — so `a + b` → `a--b` (spaces
404	on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` → `a-b` (only trailing space on
405	`:`). General markdown reference:
406	[markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub
407	publishes no official spec for auto-generated anchors; the
408	de-facto reference implementation is
409	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
410	
411	### Todo format
412	
413	`todo.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo`
414	(strict priority rank, #1 highest; long-tail backlog in
415	[todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`,
416	`## Bugs` (pointer to [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md)), and
417	`## Done` sections. Each item is a short description with
418	reference links to more detail.
419	
420	`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` …
421	numbers in the source. For `## Todo` the number is its
422	**priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs`
423	it's just an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance
424	"let's do #1" — **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
425	reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then
426	`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and normalizes
427	continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional.
428	**To refer to a Todo durably, name it by its title — a
429	plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
430	renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has
431	no anchor to link to.
432	
433	Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links
434	difficult and fragile — especially an external reference
435	pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list
436	renumbers. A robust fix (a number-free anchor, or a
437	number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
438	wildcards the numeric prefix — a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is
439	encoded, not opaque, so the title is recoverable) is a
440	`validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.
441	
442	`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews; `vc-x1 validate-todo`
443	is the read-only check. The `## Done` section keeps `-`
444	bullets — items aren't referenced by number once completed.
445	
446	Example shape:
447	
448	```
449	# Todo
450	1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
451	2. Fix bug Y [[1]]
452	
453	# Done
454	- Fixed issue Z [[2]],[[3]]
455	
456	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
457	[2]: issues.md#issue-z
458	[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
459	```
460	
461	### Retiring Done entries
462	
463	`todo.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently
464	shipped work, not a permanent log. Move entries into `done.md`
465	at two natural beats:
466	
467	- **Closing a ladder** — when the final `X.Y.Z` (no suffix)
468	  commit ships, decide which prior entries are no longer
469	  needed for nearby context and migrate them.
470	- **Opening a new ladder** — at `X.Y.Z-0`, do the same sweep
471	  before bumping the version-of-record.
472	
473	Migration mechanics:
474	
475	- Move the bullet itself from `todo.md > ## Done` to
476	  `done.md` (preserving the original ref number).
477	- Copy any references the moved entries cite into
478	  `done.md`'s `# References` section (those refs are
479	  file-local, so coexisting with `todo.md`'s namespace is
480	  fine).
481	- Prune any references in `todo.md > # References` no longer
482	  cited by anything in `## In Progress` / `## Todo` /
483	  `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.
484	
485	## Chores conventions
486	
487	### Headings and entries that record a commit
488	
489	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records — see
490	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit)
491	for the rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is
492	used for the matching `todo.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]`
493	reference to that section. Titles carry **no `(<version>)`
494	suffix** — see
495	[Commit description](notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description)
496	for why.
497	E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader`
498	and the Done line `- refactor: extract config loader [[3]]`.
499	The `## Done` entry uses the close-out commit's title.
500	
501	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`,
502	`## In Progress`, `# References`) or to design `###` subsections
503	inside a chores section — those are named for whatever fits.
504	Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong
505	default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to
506	line a record up with its commit.
507	
508	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in
509	progress; the *last* edit before `vc-x1 push` syncs it — and the
510	`## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit — to the final
511	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links)
512	for the slug algorithm; the pre-commit checklist catches a
513	dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should too
514	(and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
515	
516	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate
517	this convention keep their free-form text; the convention
518	applies going forward.
519	
520	### Chores section content — no edit list; git is the record
521	
522	A chores section is: a `Commits:` line (first line under the
523	header — see below), then [Prose form](#prose-form) (intro +
524	bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###` design
525	subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** — design points,
526	structural notes — never a per-file edit list. That lives in the
527	commit message body, which is the source of truth for "what
528	changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally
529	scoped to the commit). The chores section is the source of truth
530	for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither restates the
531	other.
532	
533	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism,
534	hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it — promote that to its
535	own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the
536	wrinkle is a live design concern (something that *should*
537	change, not just be recorded), also add a `notes/todo.md` item
538	with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo→chores is the
539	normal ref direction).
540	
541	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified
542	to be the same content in two places — and detail written twice
543	drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
544	narrative; `Commits:` links them.
545	
546	### Chores commit references
547	
548	The first line under a chores section header is a `Commits:`
549	line citing the git commit(s) that section records:
550	
551	```
552	## refactor: extract config loader
553	
554	Commits: [[3]]
555	
556	<intro paragraph...>
557	```
558	
559	`Commits:` uses the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
560	[Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)),
561	**double-bracketed** so the brackets render — `Commits: [[3]]`,
562	or `Commits: [[3]],[[5]]` for several. (`[[3]]` shows as a
563	literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner
564	`[3]` resolves against its `[3]:` definition — CommonMark /
565	GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The `# References` definition
566	puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
567	40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
568	
569	```
570	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
571	```
572	
573	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub /
574	  GitLab resolve a unique prefix to the canonical commit page
575	  (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
576	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous —
577	  it survives a repo host change, `git show <40-hex>` works in
578	  any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a
579	  database, say) gets the canonical identifier.
580	
581	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a
582	**permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived release/patch
583	branch) — a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
584	can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later:
585	every section opens with an **empty `Commits:`**, and each push
586	backfills the `Commits:` of the commits the previous push made
587	permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch
588	lands. The commit itself is the record, and
589	`git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
590	[Commits backfill](notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
591	
592	## Cycle Protocol
593	
594	Every change runs as a **cycle**: Preparation (`X.Y.Z-0`) →
595	Work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …) → Close-out (bare
596	`X.Y.Z`). Each commit runs through a per-commit flow whose
597	validation step is medium-specific — the Rust example is the
598	cargo cycle (fmt → clippy → test → install); skip-able for
599	notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. The full protocol
600	— numbering, per-commit flow, reviewing changes, close-out,
601	pushing, ochid trailers, sub-cycles — lives in
602	[`notes/cycle-protocol.md`](notes/cycle-protocol.md). Read
603	it before any commit work — and before any push, cycle or
604	not: pushes always need per-push user approval (see
605	[Pushing policy](notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy)).
606	
607	**Versioning.** How this repo numbers cycles, where the
608	version-of-record lives, and its bump cadence are
609	project-specific and documented in
610	[versioning.md](notes/versioning.md) — the single source of
611	truth that AGENTS.md and cycle-protocol.md refer to
612	abstractly.
613	
614	**Hard stop after push/finalize.** Once a push or `.claude`
615	finalize is invoked (`vc-x1 push` does both), do no further
616	work — no verification, no summary, no next-step offers —
617	until the user speaks. Put all closing words *before* the
618	invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
619	visible token after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare
620	acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed") — never a summary or more
621	work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's
622	direction. See
623	[After push or finalize](notes/cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-finalize-stop-and-wait).
624	
625	**`vc-x1 push` behaviors to keep in mind.** Two, independent
626	of project language:
627	
628	- **Preflight** runs the cargo cycle (fmt → clippy → test). On
629	  a cargo project it works as-is, so `vc-x1 push <bookmark>`
630	  runs it before the review gate. On a project with no cargo
631	  cycle — or any time preflight can't run — invoke `vc-x1 push
632	  <bookmark> --from message ...` to skip preflight and the
633	  interactive review gate, doing the diff review in
634	  conversation first.
635	- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself —
636	  don't hand-write them into the commit body or
637	  `--title`/`--body`.
638	
639	
640	## Code Conventions
641	
642	### Doc comments on every file, function, and method
643	
644	Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every
645	function and method must have a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief —
646	one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline is that the
647	comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
648	[Prose form](#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).
649	
650	This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments"
651	default that applies to inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the
652	module / item surface are expected; inline explanatory comments
653	inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
654	non-obvious WHY.
655	
656	**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive
657	`--help` output. Clap reflows by default and collapses bullets
658	into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
659	any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- …` lands on
660	its own line in the rendered help.
661	
662	### `// OK: …` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)
663	
664	Non-test code that calls `.unwrap()`, `.unwrap_or(…)`,
665	`.unwrap_or_default()`, or `.unwrap_or_else(…)` must have a trailing
666	`// OK: …` comment that justifies why the call is acceptable.
667	
668	- `// OK: <specific reason>` — document the real precondition,
669	  invariant, or domain reason. Preferred whenever the reason isn't
670	  self-evident.
671	- `// OK: obvious` — the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
672	  `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")` — empty desc → empty title).
673	
674	Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment).
675	Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are not used because they require a decoder
676	ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
677	
678	For provably-unreachable `.unwrap()` calls, also prefix with
679	`#[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]` so the site stays silent if we enable
680	the project-wide `clippy::unwrap_used` lint later.
681	
682	```rust
683	let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
684	let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious
685	
686	match matches.len() {
687	    1 => {
688	        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
689	        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
690	        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
691	    }
692	    // ...
693	}
694	```
695	
696	Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt — panicking on setup failure is the
697	correct test behavior.
698	
699	### Ask for clarification on ambiguous input
700	
701	When user input is ambiguous or missing necessary detail, stop and
702	ask a specific question. Do not proceed on a guess and hope the
703	result lands right — a clarifying question costs a few seconds;
704	redoing misaligned work costs much more.
705	
706	### Recognize when stuck
707	
708	If a simple task has eaten 5+ minutes of thinking or back-and-forth
709	without progress, stop. Summarize what's blocking — unclear
710	requirements, unfamiliar API surface, conflicting signals — and ask.
711	Continued flailing produces worse outcomes than a direct "I'm stuck
712	on X."
713

# AGENTS.md - Bot Instructions

## Project Structure

This project uses **two separate jj-git repos**:

1. **App repo** (`/` — project root): the project's generated
   artifact — code, prose, image, song, whatever it produces.
2. **Bot session repo** (`/.claude/`): Contains Claude Code session data.

Both repos are managed with `jj` (Jujutsu), which coexists with git.

**Committing vs pushing.** Default to `vc-x1 push` — it commits and
publishes both repos together, each carrying one `ochid:` pointing at
the other (see [Cycle Protocol](#cycle-protocol) and
[ochid trailers](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). Use a bare
`jj commit` (see [jj Basics](#jj-basics)) only when:

- the change will never be published — no `ochid:`;
- the commit will be squashed away before its series is pushed
  (loop-and-squash) — no `ochid:`; it disappears in the squash;
- the commit will be pushed later as a non-top commit — `jj commit`
  and add its `ochid:` now, because `vc-x1 push` stamps only the
  topmost commit it pushes, never the ancestors.

**What "commit" and "push" mean.** In an instruction, "commit",
"push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push` — land *and*
publish — unless stated otherwise. A bare `jj commit` is asked for
by name: "local commit", "save locally", "just `jj commit`" (the
cases above). So the spoken default is publish; the local-only
save is the named exception. The approval around a push —
interactive by default, waived only by an explicit scoped
delegation — is the cycle protocol's
[Pushing policy](notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Repo Paths (relative from project root)

- App repo: `.` (project root)
- Bot session repo: `.claude`
  (symlink from `~/.claude/projects/<path-to-project-root>/.claude`)

## Working Directory

Prefer staying in the project root. Use `-R` flags or absolute paths
to target other directories rather than `cd`. If `cd` seems necessary,
discuss with the user first — losing track of cwd causes subtle
command failures downstream.

When invoking shell commands, prefer the shortest unambiguous path —
usually relative to cwd (`ls notes/`, not
`ls /home/wink/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1/notes/`). Long absolute paths
clutter the transcript without adding information. Out-of-workspace
paths (`/tmp/...`, `~/.config/...`) stay absolute. Read/Edit/Write
tool args also stay absolute — that's a tool-boundary constraint,
not a stylistic choice.

Run **one command per shell invocation** — don't bundle several
steps into a single compound script (`a && b; c`). Bundling hides
which step produced which output and makes a failure ambiguous;
executing one at a time keeps the details visible and reviewable.
Exceptions are a genuine pipeline (`grep | sort`) or a tight,
inseparable pair where the join is the point.

## File reads — read the slice you need

Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the
slice your task needs; grep or read further on demand.

- **`notes/todo.md`** (the routine acquaint read) — first
  ~60 lines covers intro + `## In Progress` + the top of the
  ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`; read
  further only when chasing a lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a
  `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`** — the long-tail backlog
  (lower-priority entries below the ranked `## Todo`). Read
  only when picking up a backlog item; grep to locate it
  first.
- **`notes/bugs.md`** — the bug list. Small; read whole
  when triaging a bug or chasing the `## Bugs` pointer in
  todo.md.
- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`** —
  historical / append-mostly. Scan headings first
  (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only
  the section you need.

**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `notes/todo.md`
grows every cycle, so the backlog and bugs live in sibling
files rather than inline; the same "slice you need" rule
applies to historical files.

## Memory

Do not use the bot's per-project memory directory
(`~/.claude/projects/<path>/memory/`). In a dual-repo setup with
AGENTS.md it provides no capability AGENTS.md doesn't already cover,
and it loses on discoverability:

- **AGENTS.md** — at the repo root, a well-known location for bot
  instructions, committed, reviewable, visible to every collaborator
  (human or bot).
- **Memory directory** — hidden under the user's home, tied to one
  machine, invisible to anyone but the bot, never diffed or reviewed.

Easy for everyone to find beats convenient for the bot alone. Put
durable context in AGENTS.md (or committed `notes/`) instead.

## Plain synopsis after technical explanations

When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation
(measurement theory, statistics, hardware behavior), end it
with a short plain-language synopsis — no jargon, no symbols —
so the reader can check their understanding against the
technical version.

**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread;
the plain form catches misunderstandings early, when they are
cheap.

**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (notes
link to design.md, which should already lead with the why).
Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is
already plain needs no synopsis.

## Speculation marker

Durable text the bot writes — AGENTS.md, `notes/`, commit bodies,
chores sections — should stick to observations and direct descriptions
of the code or data. If a mechanism, hypothesis, or causal claim
enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
reader can tell the measured from the inferred.

**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader
(or the bot on a later session) can pick it up as a known fact when
it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction worth keeping visible
in the written record.

**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no
marker. Prefix with "We think ..." (or a close variant like
"Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism ("X wins
because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal
state"), a prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any
reasoning not directly supported by the data on hand.

## jj Basics

**Use jj, not git, for version-control operations** (status, log,
diff, commit, push, history rewrite). jj coexists with the git
backend, so the repo *can* be driven with raw `git`, but this
project's workflow — bookmarks, the working-copy `@` model, ochid
trailers — is expressed in jj terms; reaching for `git` invites
state that doesn't match the jj documentation here. There is no
`jj mv`: to move/rename a tracked file, just `mv` it on disk and
jj detects the rename by content.

- `jj st -R .` / `jj st -R .claude` — show working copy status
- `jj log -R .` / `jj log -R .claude` — show commit log
- `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>` — finalize working copy into a commit
- `jj describe -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>` — set description without committing
- `jj git push --bookmark <name> -R <repo>` — push a bookmark (no
  `--allow-new` flag; jj pushes new bookmarks without special flags)
- In jj, the working copy (@) is always a mutable commit being edited.
  `jj commit` finalizes it and creates a new empty working copy on top.
- The `.claude` repo always has uncommitted changes during an active
  session because session data updates continuously.
- `jj rebase` uses `--onto`/`-o` to name the destination(s).

## Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)

The cross-reference between the app repo and the `.claude` bot
repo is what makes the dual-repo work: every commit points at its
counterpart in the other repo, so the "what" (code) and the
"why / how" (session) stay linked across time. That pointer is the
**ochid** (Other Change ID) git trailer.

A **chid** is jj's change ID — a permanent identifier that
survives rebases and `describe`s (unlike the commit ID / git SHA,
which changes on rewrite). An **ochid** trailer carries the
counterpart commit's chid as a workspace-root-relative path:

- Paths start with `/` — the workspace root, i.e. the app repo
  (vc-template-x1). `/.claude` is the bot session sub-repo.
- `ochid: /<chid>` references a change in the **app repo**.
- `ochid: /.claude/<chid>` references a change in the **`.claude`
  repo**.

Trailers are blank-line-separated `key: value` lines at the end of
the commit body, using the chid's **12-character** prefix:

```
ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqowktp   # points to a .claude repo change
ochid: /wtpmottvxqzl           # points to an app repo change
```

How many, and which direction:

- **Code-side commits** each carry one
  `ochid: /.claude/<.claude-chid>` — the `.claude` change ID.
- **The `.claude` commit** carries one `ochid: /<code-chid>` per
  code commit in that push. More than one occurs on a Merge
  non-ff close-out (one ochid per Work commit in the cycle).

Use `vc-x1 chid -s code,bot -L` to capture the change IDs (first
line app, second `.claude`).

### Resolvability

A change ID travels with its commit: a **pushed** commit resolves
to the same chid in every clone — cloning the `.claude` repo gave
the published `main` tip the same chid as an existing clone. We
think jj carries the change ID in the git commit object, so it
survives `jj git clone` / fetch.

The local-only case is the **working-copy `@`**: jj mints a fresh
random chid for `@` in each clone, so an unpushed `@` is never a
stable ochid target. This is why a `.claude` ochid names `@-`
(the last committed change), not `@`.

### .vc-config.toml

Each repo contains a `.vc-config.toml` that identifies its
location within the workspace, so tools resolve these paths
without repeating the workspace path in every trailer:

```toml
# In vc-template-x1 (workspace root):
[workspace]
path = "/"

# In .claude (sub-repo):
[workspace]
path = "/.claude"
```

## Prose form

Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro
that explains the *why* or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet
list for the details. Wrap lines at ≤72 cols (bullet continuations
indent two spaces). Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs — they hide the
structure that bullets make scannable.

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files —
  see [Doc comments](#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both app-repo and session-repo). The
  ≤50-col title is the commit-specific add-on; see
  [Per-commit flow](notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` — see
  [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- Todo and Done entries in `notes/todo.md` when an entry needs more
  than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are still fine.

Bullet *content* differs by surface:

- **Commit bodies** — bullets are file-by-file: one bullet per file
  changed, file plus a one-line gist (e.g.
  `README.md: new Overview intro`). Source of truth for the
  mechanical edit list.
- **Chores / todo / done** — bullets are conceptual (design points,
  structural notes, the "what landed and why" at a notch above
  file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list —
  see [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- **Doc comments** — bullets are whatever structure fits (fields,
  cases, invariants).

### Problem + plan shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores section intros, and `## Todo`
entries use a sharper form of the same shape:

- **Problem statement** (the why) — one or two sentences;
  don't pad with intent, don't restate the plan.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when) — formality differs by
  surface:
  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per
    commit — see
    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit)
    for the per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering;
    formalized only when the entry is picked up into a
    cycle.

### Semicolons inside bullets

A bullet that joins multiple clauses with semicolons (`A; B; C`)
is a list hiding inside running prose — break the clauses into
sub-bullets so the structure shows. Semicolons in running prose
(intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very
short clauses or tight pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when
breaking would be more noise than signal.

### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)

A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description
share a *title* shape — a
[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/)
title over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail. They differ in the
title's prefix / marker (below) and in bullet *content* — commit
bodies are file-by-file, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet
*content* differs by surface" above). The shared template:

```
<optional - X.Y.Z[-N]> <title>   # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
<optional prose intro>
  - <optional item>
    <optional prose intro>
      - <optional sub-item>
      ...
```

The three surfaces apply it as:

- **Ladder step** (`notes/todo.md` `## In Progress`): the title is
  prefixed with the version — `X.Y.Z-N <title>` — and
  carries a `(current)` / `(done)` marker. The bare three-element
  `X.Y.Z` (no `-N`) is the close-out step. Detail is bulleted,
  never `;`-joined inline.
- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no version
  prefix — the `##` header *is* the bare title, with a
  `Commits: [[ref]]` line first under it (empty until backfilled —
  see [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references)).
- **Commit description**: no version prefix — the title is the
  ≤50-col first line; the body is the prose (file-by-file for the
  app repo, per [Per-commit flow](notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow)).

The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a
step's ladder entry, its chores `##` header, and its commit title
line up verbatim — pick the commit title first and reuse it.

That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a
cycle gets its own distinct descriptive title — never one shared
cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep
a cycle's commits collectable with one `git log --grep`, give the
step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).

## Notes file conventions

Conventions the bot follows when writing notes files
(`notes/todo.md`, `notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`,
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One source
of truth lives here; [`notes/README.md`](notes/README.md)
points back.

### Notes references

Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render
— `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]` for several (comma-separated, not
`[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)`
links stay single-bracketed.

### Reference numbering

Every note file (`todo.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`,
`chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a file-local `# References`
section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that
file — `[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md`
are independent slots that may point at completely different
URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.

Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only
meaningful within its file's `# References`. So a `[N]` *citation*
(bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another file's number; to cite a target a sibling
file references, pick your own next-local slot and define it
(the same target may carry a different number in each file). A
`[N]` *inside a code span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different — that's
a quoted identifier: literal text naming a ref-key (often from
another file's namespace), data, not a citation; it needs no
definition here. To point at a section of another file from
prose, use an inline link with an anchor —
`[that section](../chores-07.md#…)` — not a bare number.

A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a
`/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or `/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may
also be a **commit reference** —
`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by
a section's `Commits:` line. See
[Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the
why and the exact shape.

A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous
`[1]..[N]` in first-citation-appearance order — walk the file's
prose in document order (`todo.md`: `## Todo` then `## Done`;
`chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first
`[[N]]` citation appears. This is a file-local rewrite — only
that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:` definitions move; every
target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` ``
code span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone.
Do it opportunistically (when the namespace has drifted enough to
annoy), not on a schedule: `todo.md` fragments fastest (entries
land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate;
`chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are append-mostly and only need it
after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated slots
out of document order).

### Markdown anchor links

GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric
characters in place, map remaining spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do
**not** collapse adjacent whitespace — so `a + b` → `a--b` (spaces
on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` → `a-b` (only trailing space on
`:`). General markdown reference:
[markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub
publishes no official spec for auto-generated anchors; the
de-facto reference implementation is
[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).

### Todo format

`todo.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo`
(strict priority rank, #1 highest; long-tail backlog in
[todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`,
`## Bugs` (pointer to [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md)), and
`## Done` sections. Each item is a short description with
reference links to more detail.

`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` …
numbers in the source. For `## Todo` the number is its
**priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs`
it's just an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance
"let's do #1" — **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then
`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and normalizes
continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional.
**To refer to a Todo durably, name it by its title — a
plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has
no anchor to link to.

Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links
difficult and fragile — especially an external reference
pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list
renumbers. A robust fix (a number-free anchor, or a
number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
wildcards the numeric prefix — a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is
encoded, not opaque, so the title is recoverable) is a
`validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.

`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews; `vc-x1 validate-todo`
is the read-only check. The `## Done` section keeps `-`
bullets — items aren't referenced by number once completed.

Example shape:

```
# Todo
1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
2. Fix bug Y [[1]]

# Done
- Fixed issue Z [[2]],[[3]]

[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
[2]: issues.md#issue-z
[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
```

### Retiring Done entries

`todo.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently
shipped work, not a permanent log. Move entries into `done.md`
at two natural beats:

- **Closing a ladder** — when the final `X.Y.Z` (no suffix)
  commit ships, decide which prior entries are no longer
  needed for nearby context and migrate them.
- **Opening a new ladder** — at `X.Y.Z-0`, do the same sweep
  before bumping the version-of-record.

Migration mechanics:

- Move the bullet itself from `todo.md > ## Done` to
  `done.md` (preserving the original ref number).
- Copy any references the moved entries cite into
  `done.md`'s `# References` section (those refs are
  file-local, so coexisting with `todo.md`'s namespace is
  fine).
- Prune any references in `todo.md > # References` no longer
  cited by anything in `## In Progress` / `## Todo` /
  `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.

## Chores conventions

### Headings and entries that record a commit

A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records — see
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit)
for the rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is
used for the matching `todo.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]`
reference to that section. Titles carry **no `(<version>)`
suffix** — see
[Commit description](notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description)
for why.
E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader`
and the Done line `- refactor: extract config loader [[3]]`.
The `## Done` entry uses the close-out commit's title.

This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`,
`## In Progress`, `# References`) or to design `###` subsections
inside a chores section — those are named for whatever fits.
Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong
default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to
line a record up with its commit.

A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in
progress; the *last* edit before `vc-x1 push` syncs it — and the
`## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit — to the final
commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links)
for the slug algorithm; the pre-commit checklist catches a
dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should too
(and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).

Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate
this convention keep their free-form text; the convention
applies going forward.

### Chores section content — no edit list; git is the record

A chores section is: a `Commits:` line (first line under the
header — see below), then [Prose form](#prose-form) (intro +
bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###` design
subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** — design points,
structural notes — never a per-file edit list. That lives in the
commit message body, which is the source of truth for "what
changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally
scoped to the commit). The chores section is the source of truth
for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither restates the
other.

When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism,
hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it — promote that to its
own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the
wrinkle is a live design concern (something that *should*
change, not just be recorded), also add a `notes/todo.md` item
with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo→chores is the
normal ref direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified
to be the same content in two places — and detail written twice
drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
narrative; `Commits:` links them.

### Chores commit references

The first line under a chores section header is a `Commits:`
line citing the git commit(s) that section records:

```
## refactor: extract config loader

Commits: [[3]]

<intro paragraph...>
```

`Commits:` uses the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
[Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)),
**double-bracketed** so the brackets render — `Commits: [[3]]`,
or `Commits: [[3]],[[5]]` for several. (`[[3]]` shows as a
literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner
`[3]` resolves against its `[3]:` definition — CommonMark /
GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The `# References` definition
puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub /
  GitLab resolve a unique prefix to the canonical commit page
  (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous —
  it survives a repo host change, `git show <40-hex>` works in
  any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a
  database, say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a
**permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived release/patch
branch) — a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later:
every section opens with an **empty `Commits:`**, and each push
backfills the `Commits:` of the commits the previous push made
permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch
lands. The commit itself is the record, and
`git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
[Commits backfill](notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

## Cycle Protocol

Every change runs as a **cycle**: Preparation (`X.Y.Z-0`) →
Work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …) → Close-out (bare
`X.Y.Z`). Each commit runs through a per-commit flow whose
validation step is medium-specific — the Rust example is the
cargo cycle (fmt → clippy → test → install); skip-able for
notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. The full protocol
— numbering, per-commit flow, reviewing changes, close-out,
pushing, ochid trailers, sub-cycles — lives in
[`notes/cycle-protocol.md`](notes/cycle-protocol.md). Read
it before any commit work — and before any push, cycle or
not: pushes always need per-push user approval (see
[Pushing policy](notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy)).

**Versioning.** How this repo numbers cycles, where the
version-of-record lives, and its bump cadence are
project-specific and documented in
[versioning.md](notes/versioning.md) — the single source of
truth that AGENTS.md and cycle-protocol.md refer to
abstractly.

**Hard stop after push/finalize.** Once a push or `.claude`
finalize is invoked (`vc-x1 push` does both), do no further
work — no verification, no summary, no next-step offers —
until the user speaks. Put all closing words *before* the
invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
visible token after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare
acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed") — never a summary or more
work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's
direction. See
[After push or finalize](notes/cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-finalize-stop-and-wait).

**`vc-x1 push` behaviors to keep in mind.** Two, independent
of project language:

- **Preflight** runs the cargo cycle (fmt → clippy → test). On
  a cargo project it works as-is, so `vc-x1 push <bookmark>`
  runs it before the review gate. On a project with no cargo
  cycle — or any time preflight can't run — invoke `vc-x1 push
  <bookmark> --from message ...` to skip preflight and the
  interactive review gate, doing the diff review in
  conversation first.
- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself —
  don't hand-write them into the commit body or
  `--title`/`--body`.


## Code Conventions

### Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every
function and method must have a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief —
one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline is that the
comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments"
default that applies to inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the
module / item surface are expected; inline explanatory comments
inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive
`--help` output. Clap reflows by default and collapses bullets
into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- …` lands on
its own line in the rendered help.

### `// OK: …` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

Non-test code that calls `.unwrap()`, `.unwrap_or(…)`,
`.unwrap_or_default()`, or `.unwrap_or_else(…)` must have a trailing
`// OK: …` comment that justifies why the call is acceptable.

- `// OK: <specific reason>` — document the real precondition,
  invariant, or domain reason. Preferred whenever the reason isn't
  self-evident.
- `// OK: obvious` — the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
  `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")` — empty desc → empty title).

Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment).
Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are not used because they require a decoder
ring for readers seeing the code out of context.

For provably-unreachable `.unwrap()` calls, also prefix with
`#[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]` so the site stays silent if we enable
the project-wide `clippy::unwrap_used` lint later.

```rust
let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious

match matches.len() {
    1 => {
        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt — panicking on setup failure is the
correct test behavior.

### Ask for clarification on ambiguous input

When user input is ambiguous or missing necessary detail, stop and
ask a specific question. Do not proceed on a guess and hope the
result lands right — a clarifying question costs a few seconds;
redoing misaligned work costs much more.

### Recognize when stuck

If a simple task has eaten 5+ minutes of thinking or back-and-forth
without progress, stop. Summarize what's blocking — unclear
requirements, unfamiliar API surface, conflicting signals — and ask.
Continued flailing produces worse outcomes than a direct "I'm stuck
on X."

content.text:
Good context — and to be safe: vc-x1's old AGENTS.md with those definitions is still recoverable at its `@-` (my overwrite only touched the working copy), and I have its text in context. Its definition block was:

> 1. **Work repo** (`/` — project root): Contains the application source code.
> 2. **Bot repo** (`/.claude/`): Contains Claude Code session data.

I also checked how the terminology actually lives in vc-x1 today. Thoughts:

**Standardizing is worth doing regardless of which names win.** The consolidated AGENTS.md currently mixes at least six variants: "App repo", "Bot session repo", "bot repo" (ochid intro), "session repo" (Prose form), "`.claude` repo", and "Code-side commits". That's exactly the kind of drift a single definitions block fixes.

**"Bot repo" is an easy yes.** It's already the dominant term across vc-x1's living notes (bot-data-formats.md, forks-multi-user.md, chores-13, todo.md all say "bot repo"), it matches the CLI's scope name `bot`, and it's shorter than "bot session repo". One distinction worth writing into the definition: `.claude` is the bot repo's *path*, not its name — commands (`-R .claude`) and ochid paths (`/.claude/<chid>`) keep the literal path.

**"Work repo" is the right call too, with two frictions to accept consciously:**

Prose saying "work repo" while every quoted command says `code` forces readers to hold a work↔code mapping. Two ways out: state the mapping once in the definitions block ("the CLI's scope name for the work repo is `code`"), or eventually rename/alias the scope to `work` (keeping `code` for compat) — that's a vc-x1 cycle of its own. I'd do the former now, and put the alias on the todo list.

content.text:
Hyphenation has a standard answer in English, and I'd follow it rather than invent a project rule: **hyphenate in attributive position, open everywhere else.**

- As nouns, keep them open: "the work repo", "the bot repo". "Work-repo" as a standalone noun is nonstandard and would read oddly; it would also fight the entire existing corpus — vc-x1's notes say "bot repo" unhyphenated everywhere (bot-data-formats.md, forks-multi-user.md, chores, todo).
- As modifiers, hyphenate: "work-repo commits", "bot-repo side", "a work-repo-only flag". That's the ordinary compound-modifier rule, and the consolidated AGENTS.md already does it in places ("app-repo and session-repo" bodies, "code-repo-only" in vc-x1's todo).

One real wrinkle your "work commit" example surfaces: **bare "work commit" is genuinely ambiguous, and I'd avoid it entirely** rather than standardize it. The cycle protocol already owns "Work commit" / "Work-N" as a term of art meaning a specific cycle stage (`X.Y.Z-1`, `-2`, …) — and Preparation and Close-out commits are *also* commits in the work repo but are not Work commits. So "work commit" can't safely mean "commit in the work repo." The hyphen rule resolves this cleanly:

- **Work commit / Work-N** (capitalized, no hyphen before "commit") — the cycle-stage term, unchanged.
- **work-repo commit** (hyphenated attributive) — any commit landing in the work repo, when you need the generic.

This is where hyphenation actually earns its keep — distinguishing those two — rather than as a blanket spelling.

On grep-ability (the usual argument for always-hyphenating): under this rule there are two spellings, but `grep -Ei 'work[- ]repo'` catches both, so nothing is lost. A blanket "always hyphenate" would buy one canonical spelling at the cost of unnatural noun usage and a large sweep of existing "bot repo" text — not worth it.

So the definitions block would say: **work repo** and **bot repo** (open compounds; hyphenate only as modifiers: "work-repo commit", "bot-repo side"), with "Work commit / Work-N" reserved for the cycle stage.

content.text:
Simpler than it sounds. The question to ask is: **is another noun coming right after the phrase, or is the phrase itself the thing?**

- **The phrase is the thing** (it's the noun of the sentence) → no hyphen:
  - "push the **work repo**"
  - "the **bot repo** always has uncommitted changes"
  - "clone both the work repo and the bot repo"

  Here "work repo" is what the sentence is about — you could put "the" in front of it and stop.

- **The phrase describes the next word** (another noun follows immediately) → hyphen:
  - "a **work-repo** commit" — the thing is the *commit*; "work-repo" just says which kind
  - "the **bot-repo** side of the push" — the thing is the *side*
  - "a **work-repo-only** flag" — the thing is the *flag*

The mechanical test: **look at the word right after "repo". If it's another noun ("commit", "side", "flag", "history"), hyphenate. If it's not (a verb, a period, "and", "is"…), leave it open.**

Why the hyphen exists at all: it prevents a misparse. In "work repo commit", a reader can momentarily group it as "work (repo commit)" — the hyphen in "work-repo commit" glues the first two words together so the grouping is unambiguous. When nothing follows, there's nothing to misgroup, so no hyphen is needed.

Same rule you already know from other writing: "the error is well known" vs. "a well-known error"; "runs at compile time" vs. "a compile-time check".

If you want, when we do the sweep I can phrase it in the definitions block without the grammar jargon, something like: *"work repo" and "bot repo" are written as two words; add a hyphen only when the pair sits directly in front of another noun ("work-repo commit", "bot-repo side").*

# Chores-01.md

1	# Cycle protocol
2	
3	This protocol uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
4	contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.
5	
6	The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
7	the conversation — code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
8	The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
9	cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
10	equivalents — this project's manifest is recorded in
11	[versioning.md](versioning.md).
12	
13	## Cycles
14	
15	A cycle has three phases:
16	
17	- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`) — the cycle's
18	  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
19	  it and starts at `-1` — see
20	  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
21	  cycle:

23	    and the suffix scheme are project-specific — see
24	    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
25	  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
26	    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
27	    statement + plan ladder).
28	  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
29	- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …) — the
30	  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
31	  needs; each runs through the
32	  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
33	- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`) — the cycle's
34	  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
35	  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
36	    `## Done`.
37	  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
38	    [chores section](#chores-sections).
39	  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
40	    changed.
41	
42	A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
43	either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
44	result must always be published at close-out. See
45	[Pushing](#pushing).
46	
47	**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to

55	## Chores sections
56	
57	A **chores section** is a `##` section in
58	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
59	general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
60	should have a reference to it on a `Commits:` list in a
61	chores file.
62	
63	The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a
64	`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
65	with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`),
66	followed by an **empty `Commits:`** line. The narrative
67	body stays empty until close-out (see [Close-out](#close-out));
68	the `Commits:` line is backfilled later, once the commit is
69	permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).
70	
71	Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
72	design subsection pattern, `Commits:` formatting) live in
73	AGENTS.md [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions).
74	
75	### Commits backfill
76	
77	A chores section's `Commits:` line cites the commit(s) it
78	records, by SHA — but a SHA isn't stable until the commit
79	lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
80	release/patch branch that won't be rewritten); a rebase or
81	squash rewrites it on the way. So:
82	
83	- A chores section is **opened with an empty `Commits:`** line.
84	- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**,
85	  where its SHA is final. A commit can't record its own SHA
86	  (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one
87	  push later: **each push backfills the `Commits:` of the
88	  commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
89	  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands —
90	  so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
91	  invalidate.
92	
93	Use `[[N]]` refs — several as `[[N]],[[M]]` only when one
94	section records multiple commits (a merge non-ff close-out) —

96	(format in AGENTS.md
97	[Chores commit references](../AGENTS.md#chores-commit-references)).
98	A section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a rare
99	deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
100	`git log --grep "<title>"`.
101	
102	The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma — a
103	**per-close-out** model (recording a cycle's SHAs at its
104	close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded
105	SHA must be permanent.
106	
107	## Preparation
108	
109	The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs
110	setup (a lightweight cycle omits it — see

142	## Close-out

content.content:
Work commit:

1. **Rebase the close-out into a merge** — `jj rebase -r
   <closeout> --onto <prev> --onto <work-tip>`.
   - `-r <closeout>` keeps the `<closeout>` commit in place.
   - `--onto <prev>` becomes its first parent (trunk).
   - `--onto <work-tip>` becomes the second parent.

   Together these make `<closeout>` a merge of
   `<prev>` + `<work-tip>`, forming a trapezoidal commit.
2. **Use `jj new <merge>`** to add an empty `@` above the
   merge. The rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing
   merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted;
   `jj new` restores the clean empty `@` on top.
3. **Push** — `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.

**Post-hoc caveat.** If the cycle was already pushed
[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) its commits are
immutable: the rebase needs `--ignore-immutable` and the
push force-updates `main`.
The standard sequence assumes the merge is set up *before*
the close-out push.

### vc-x1 push wrapper

`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
work-repo bookmark only; the bot repo is always pinned to
`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).

**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other
shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
project state, tracked in the project's `notes/todo.md` —
this protocol describes only the stable mechanism.

### .claude cadence

Everything in the manifest checks out. My assessment, no changes made:

**Verdict: I agree with all eight corrections and would adopt the vc-x1 candidate text verbatim.** The template's text was describing pre-0.69.0 tool behavior, and the corrections are verified, not just asserted.

**Verification results** (everything the manifest claims, I checked):

- The AGENTS.md and cycle-protocol.md diffs against the template contain exactly the declared corrections — nothing undeclared rode along.
- `versioning.md` and `jj-tips.md` are byte-identical to the template's, as claimed.
- Source checks pass: `stage_preflight` in push.rs does only bookmark-tracking verification, the bot-published invariant, and `sync --check` — no build or tests, so the preflight rewrite is accurate. Stage names are `push-work` / `squash-push-bot`, and the squash-push log strings confirm it runs in-process, matching the new Recovery text ("visible non-zero exit — no log file to chase").

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - 0.xx.y close-out and validation

## Todo

 Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,
 descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
 `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run notes/todo.md` to renumber.
 The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs — to refer
 to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention;
 a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its
 number. Long-tail entries
 live in [todo-backlog.md](todo-backlog.md). Use the
 [Prose Form in AGENTS.md](/AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper
 detail goes in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design
 subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. **Move `notes/todo.md` to `./TODO.md`.** The todo list is
   the project's live state and the routine acquaint read;
   root-level uppercase puts it in the conventional root-file
   family (README, LICENSE, AGENTS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md) —
   the same "easy for everyone to find" argument that put
   AGENTS.md at the root. Siblings (`todo-backlog.md`,
   `bugs.md`, `done.md`) stay in `notes/` — TODO.md is the
   entry point, the README→docs/ shape.
   - Reference churn: TODO.md's relative links gain `notes/`
     prefixes; inbound links in `notes/README.md` and
     `refactor-20260716.md` update; historical chores
     mentions stay as-is.
   - The AGENTS.md "File reads" section is part of the
     shared verbatim set, so this is a three-project change
     (vc-x1, vc-template-x1, iiac-perf) applied identically —
     sequence it *after* the in-flight notes-sync review
     round lands.
   - Sweep src/ doc strings / help text naming
     `notes/todo.md` (the tools take the path as an arg, so
     code behavior is unaffected).
   - Decision (2026-07-16): shared AGENTS.md keeps hard
     paths (greppable) rather than naming the file
     abstractly.
2. **Refactor: typed jj facade → jj-lib in-process; end
   subprocess spawning.** Version-control operations are
   ~30 hand-rolled `run("jj", …)` spawns plus every
   mutation, with per-module private wrappers and raw-git
   vestiges in init — stderr parsing instead of typed
   errors, and jj's single-attempt index-lock acquisition
   (the push `bookmark-set` lock race in [bugs.md](bugs.md))
   can't be retried where it fails. A multi-ladder program;
   the staged plan, design detail, and the eight absorbed
   former Todos live in
   [refactor-20260716.md](refactor-20260716.md).
   - Stages in execution order: DRY facade → hygiene
     riders → facade owns topology → de-gitify init →
     split push.rs → jj-lib migration → push body-intro
     validation → trapezoid close-out → por → dual
     conversion.
3. **vc-x1 push: pause point between commit and publish
   stages.** The merge non-ff close-out is a three-step
   sequence:
   - commit the close-out pair locally (normal 1:1 commit
     stages, ochids injected both directions)
   - rebase the code-side close-out into the merge (chids
     survive rebase, so every ochid stays valid)
   - publish
